title: 'Look at India': Trump Cites 7% Growth to Attack Fed Over High Interest Rates
excerpt: The President held up India's low rates and 7 per cent growth as a model, called the Fed "very political," and claimed US growth could hit 20 per cent — a claim set against official data showing 3.4 per cent.
body:
• US President Donald Trump on Friday cited India's low interest rates and 7 per cent GDP growth to attack the Federal Reserve, calling it "very political" and arguing US growth could reach 15 to 20 per cent if rates were lower, ANI reported.
  • The 15 to 20 per cent figure is the President's claim, not a forecast: official US data put third-quarter growth at a 3.4 per cent annual rate, and Trump put current growth at 4 per cent in the same remarks.
  • Trump tied his case to debt costs, saying each percentage point of interest rates represents $650 billion, according to IANS.
  • For readers in the US: no rate change was announced. The remarks are presidential pressure on the Fed, not a policy decision — borrowing costs move only when the Fed itself acts.

US President Donald Trump reached for an Indian comparison to make his case against his own central bank. Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday, he cited India's low interest rates and 7 per cent GDP growth while accusing the US Federal Reserve of keeping borrowing costs too high, according to ANI, reported by Daily Prabhat.

"If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP. We'd have a 14%, 15%, maybe even a 20% GDP."

— Donald Trump, US President

"Interest rates are too high because we have a very political Fed. I'm not blaming the chairman, but the fact that we have a very political Fed. Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the interest rates. They do that for a reason. It should be the opposite," Trump said. His argument is that strong economic numbers make the United States a better credit, so rates should fall as growth strengthens — the reverse, he alleged, of what the Fed does.

"We do just the opposite. We do it to destroy the country. When we have these great numbers, you shouldn't keep raising the rates. You should lower rates because we're a better credit. We would have a GDP of 15 or 20 per cent, not 4 per cent. We'd pay off the debt very rapidly. That's the way it should work. But we do it in reverse," he said. He also argued the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world: "We're the country that makes other countries successful. Some of them are considered financial elite, but they are not. They are only elite because of us. So we should have the lowest."

The claim against the data

The growth figures in the President's remarks are his own. He put current US growth at 4 per cent and projected 14 to 20 per cent under lower rates. Official US government data, by contrast, put real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026 at an annual rate of 3.4 per cent, according to Connected to India, which also noted that the Fed raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023, defying the President's demand for cuts. Trump did not specify the period for either country's growth figure or how large a cut he thought would be needed, according to IANS, reported by The Freedom Press.

The backdrop the Fed is weighing is different from the one in the President's remarks. US inflation continues to remain well above the Federal Reserve's 2 per cent target: the annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation rate stood at 3.6 per cent in September, and core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 3.1 per cent, according to data cited by ANI. The Fed operates on a dual mandate to control inflation and maintain maximum employment.

Why he keeps returning to the debt

Trump tied his call for lower rates directly to the cost of servicing the national debt, saying a one percentage point reduction would save $650 billion and that faster growth would let the US pay down debt more rapidly, according to IANS. That arithmetic is the core of his public case: cheaper borrowing is presented not as stimulus but as a saving. Nothing in Friday's remarks changes policy. The Fed sets rates independently, and the President's comparison with India — a central bank, the RBI, operating in a faster-growing economy — is an argument about direction, not a mechanism that moves US mortgage or credit-card rates on its own.
